title: Order Splitting and Liquidity Replenishment Are Jointly Necessary for the Square-Root Law of Market Impact:

p.t: When a large institutional order (metaorder) of size Q is executed, the resulting price impact I obeys a power-law scaling: with δ ≈ 0.5 across equity markets [2,3,4,5,1]. Here V D and σ D denote daily volume and daily volatility respectively. This "square-root law" (SRL) has become an established regularity of quantitative market microstructure [6,7], yet the mechanisms that produce it remain unsettled. Four theoretical routes have been proposed. The LOB walking argument [8] notes that a market order crossing a book with cumulative profile V (q) ∼ q 1+γ produces δ = 1/(1 + γ); a parabolic book (γ = 1) gives δ = 0.5. This prediction, however, depends on the visible book shape and ignores latent orders that may appear during execution; Weber & Rosenow themselves showed that dynamic feedback reduces actual impact well below the staticbook prediction. The GGPS framework of Gabaix et al. [9] links δ to the tail exponent β of the metaorder size distribution via δ = β -1, assuming optimal execution -but the distribution alone need not determine impact if execution dynamics mediate the size-displacement relationship. The FGLW theory of Farmer et al. [10] replaces β with the child-order count tail exponent α, predicting δ = α -1; it shares the same limitation. The latent liquidity theory [11,12] takes a different route: as execution moves the price, new hidden orders are continuously revealed, yielding δ ≈ 0.5 irrespective of the visible LOB shape. This framework is elegant but difficult to test directly, since latent liquidity is by definition unobservable.

These theories make distinct, testable predictions for δ, and a natural null hypothesis is that one of them captures the relevant mechanism: that the SRL arises either from the metaorder size distribution (GGPS), from the child-order count distribution (FGLW), or from the shape of the visible limit order book (LOB walking). Existing agent-based studies have reproduced the SRL [4,12,11], but none has systematically disentangled the causal role of each mechanism through controlled ablation, nor ruled out the competing predictions on the same simulated data. The present paper tests this null hypothesis directly. We build a minimal limit-order-book ABM populated by heterogeneous interacting agents -simple enough that each mechanism can be turned on and off -and use it in two complementary ways. First, counterfactual ablation: by selectively suppressing order splitting, removing market makers, imposing price limits, or varying liquidity, we measure how δ responds and isolate the mechanisms whose removal breaks the SRL. Second, a per-stock computational stress test of the three quantitative predictions (GGPS, FGLW, LOB walking): for each of 2000 independently simulated stocks we measure the relevant exponents (β, α, γ) and compare predicted versus measured δ. The two lines of evidence converge: all three predictions are rejected on identical data, and only the ablation of splitting or of liquidity replenishment substantially destroys δ ≈ 1/2.

The simulated market is a continuous double-auction limit order book. Both market and limit orders are supported; the tick size is set to 1 basis point of the initial price, mimicking liquid equity markets.

Four agent types populate the market, each representing a class of real market participants. Institutional agents (N inst = 20) are the sole source of metaorders. Each institution draws a total order size Q from a Pareto distribution with shape ξ ∼ Uniform[1.5, 3.5] and splits Q into N c child orders that arrive as a Poisson process (λ = 3 ticks). The default splitting rule is Dirichlet. To ensure the Q/V D axis spans the empirically relevant range (0.01%-10%), the minimum order size q min is log-spaced across agents from 1 to 2000. High-frequency trading (HFT) / market-maker agents (N HFT ∈ [3, 10] per stock) post two-sided limit orders at ℓ = 50 price levels with adaptive spread. After each fill they replenish with probability p = 0.9; this provides the continuous liquidity that lets the LOB recover between child orders. Retail agents (N retail ∈ [100, 400] per stock) submit small, randomly directed market orders of size [1,10]. They play the same role as noise traders in standard microstructure models, providing background turnover. News agents (N = 3) occasionally inject large market orders. Their purpose is to generate exogenous volatility spikes, without which the simulated return distribution would lack the heavy tails seen in real markets.

We simulate N s = 2000 stocks with independently drawn parameters (20 stocks for the counterfactual experiments; see Section 4.3). Each stock receives a random initial price (log-uniform from [1000, 50000]), a random number of retail traders (Uniform[100, 400]), a random number of HFT agents (Uniform [3,10]), and a random Pareto shape ξ (Uniform[1.5, 3.5]). The tick size scales with the initial price. This cross-stock variation prevents any single parameter choice from dominating the results.

Each stock runs for T = 10 6 steps, preceded by a 5 × 10 4 -step warmup that lets the LOB self-organise. At every step one agent is chosen uniformly at random to act. Stocks are independent (separate random seeds). We checked convergence by comparing δ estimated on the first and second halves of the baseline trajectory: the two estimates agree to within ±0.01 for all 2000 stocks, confirming that 10 6 steps is sufficient for the impact exponent to stabilise. The 2000-stock baseline simulation required approximately 3 hours of wall-clock time on a 40-core Xeon E5-2698 v4 server (each stock is embarrassingly parallel).

Because the model records every trade, we reconstruct metaorders ex post by grouping consecutive same-agent, same-direction trades. Two trades from the same agent are assigned to different metaorders if they are separated by more than ∆t = 10 steps or if the direction flips. We chose ∆t = 10 because the median inter-child interval in the baseline is 3 ticks; setting the threshold at roughly three medians captures the bulk of each metaorder without overmerging distinct orders.

We normalise each metaorder by the statistics of the day on which it executes, following [1]: where D is the day-d total traded volume and σ (d) D the day-d price range (high-low). Normalising by true per-day quantities rather than aggregate averages matters because dividing by a constant V D /N days only shifts the log-log plot without changing δ.

Logarithmic binning (20 bins, ≥ 30 points per bin) converts the scatter of normalised (Q norm , I norm ) pairs into bin averages, to which we fit I = c Q δ by relative least squares: Metaorders with Q/V D < 0.01% are dropped: at such tiny sizes the measured impact is dominated by the bid-ask spread rather than by the shape of the LOB.

Before studying impact, we check that the simulated market reproduces the basic statistical signatures of real equity markets. Figure 1 shows daily candlestick charts and volume for four stocks with different parameters. Prices behave as random walks with stock-dependent volatility, as expected. At tick level (Figure 2), the simulated returns are fat-tailed (excess kurtosis κ = 29.5), negatively autocorrelated at lag 1 (autocorrelation function ACF(1)= -0.355, the classic bid-ask bounce signature [13]), and exhibit slowly decaying absolute-return autocorrelation (ACF(1)= 0.309), i.e. volatility clustering.

Figure 3 plots the impact curve for four individual stocks. Each stock yields a well-defined power law with δ ∈ [0.49, 0.61]; all bracket the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) benchmark ⟨δ⟩ = 0.489 [1]. Pooling all stocks gives δ = 0.549, c = 0.982, to be compared with ⟨δ⟩ = 0.489, ⟨c⟩ = 0.842 from [1]. To check robustness, we repeat the analysis on 2000 stocks with independently drawn parameters. The per-stock δ distribution (Figure 4) has mean 0.539 ± 0.048 and range [0.449, 0.633], while ⟨c⟩ = 0.934 ± 0.130. The TSE distribution spans a wider range ([0.2, 0.7] across 2000 stocks) because real markets vary in trading rules, investor composition, and regulatory regime -sources of variation absent from our minimal setup. Both distributions nonetheless centre on δ ≈ 1/2. Figure 5: Predicted vs. measured δ for the same 2000 baseline stocks (square panels, equal axes). Horizontal axis: measured δ; vertical axis: predicted δ. Left: GGPS (δ pred = β -1); centre: FGLW (δ pred = α -1); right: LOB walking (δ pred = 1/(1 + γ)). Diagonal: perfect agreement. Red star: cross-stock mean. All points in the left and centre panels lie above the diagonal (over-prediction); in the right panel most lie below (under-prediction). Since each of the three quantitative predictions can be evaluated on the same per-stock data, Figure 5 offers a direct, model-internal test: GGPS and FGLW predict δ > 1 in every stock (left and centre panels, all points above the diagonal), while LOB walking predicts δ < 0.5 in most stocks (right panel, below the diagonal). None of the three passes through the cloud of measured δ ≈ 0.5. The failure of all three single-mechanism predictions motivates the counterfactual experiments of Section 4.3, which identify the mechanisms that are responsible.

Table 1 collects the results of eight counterfactual scenarios, each a variant of the baseline in which one mechanism is suppressed or altered. All scenarios run 20 independent stocks (see Section 2). The table shows a clear hierarchy. Removing order splitting causes δ to collapse from 0.549 to 0.324, the largest single change among all scenarios. Without splitting, every metaorder lands as one huge market order that consumes the available depth at a single instant; the LOB has no time to recover between slices. Removing HFT agents has a similar direction (δ → 0.386) but a weaker effect: the book still receives some resting liquidity from retail limit orders, but without active replenishment the depth is thinner and impact is larger. By contrast, perturbations that leave splitting and HFT intact barely move δ. Price limits, momentum trading, reduced background liquidity, uniform splitting, and front-loaded splitting all yield δ ∈ [0.49, 0.53] -within 10% of the baseline. Figure 6 shows the impact curves for the four most illustrative scenarios, and Figure 7 summarises the fitted δ across all eight scenarios. The baseline curve is concave (δ = 0.55); the no-splitting curve is nearly flat (δ = 0.32).

We now examine in detail why each of the three predictions fails on the baseline data (Figure 5). GGPS (δ = β -1) over-predicts in every stock (δ GGPS ∈ [0.74, 1.56], mean 1.16), because the Hill estimator β captures the unconditional size tail whereas impact depends on the conditional displacement given size. FGLW (δ = α -1) fares even worse (δ FGLW ∈ [1.26, 2.47], mean 2.00); both theories predict δ > 1, far above the observed δ ≈ 0.5. LOB walking (δ = 1/(1 + γ)) goes in the opposite direction: the fitted γ ∈ [0.5, 13] is much larger than the empirical γ ≈ 1, so the prediction δ LOB ∈ [0.07, 0.69] (mean 0.36) systematically underestimates the measured δ. The visible book in our model is too concave, and the latent liquidity that Donier et al. [12] argue softens impact is not captured by a static snapshot of the LOB. No single theory reproduces δ within our model (Figure 5). The SRL appears to arise from the coupling of splitting (which creates time gaps) and liquidity replenishment (which refills the book during those gaps) -the picture suggested by the latent liquidity framework. We note that this is a computational, model-internal test; whether the same conclusion holds in real markets would require analogous empirical measurement.

Two mechanisms stand out as necessary. Order splitting is the dominant factor: its removal collapses δ from 0.549 to 0.324, well below both 1/2 and 1. The microscopic order flow explains this. In the baseline, a metaorder of size Q = 10 4 is split into, say, N c = 50 child orders arriving every λ = 3 ticks. Between children, HFT agents replenish the book at the best quotes. The cumulative impact is the sum of N c small kicks, each partially absorbed by fresh liquidity. When splitting is turned off, the same Q = 10 4 hits the book as a single market order. The LOB is traversed from the best bid (or ask) outward, and the total price displacement is set by the cumulative depth profile V (q) at the single instant of arrival. Because V (q) grows super-linearly in our model (γ ≈ 2), larger unsplit orders encounter disproportionately more depth per unit of additional size, and the resulting impact curve is concave with δ < 1/2. The precise value δ = 0.324 reflects the specific shape of the resting book at the moment of arrival -it is not a universal constant but a consequence of the model's LOB geometry. Liquidity replenishment by HFT agents is the second necessary ingredient. When HFT is removed, the book still receives resting orders from retail limit submissions, but the active two-sided quoting that refills depleted levels after each fill is gone. The LOB thins during execution, so each subsequent child order moves the price further than it would in a replenished book, producing a steeper impact curve (δ = 0.386).

Changing the splitting rule (Dirichlet, uniform, or front-loaded) has virtually no measurable effect (δ ∈ [0.49, 0.53]). Adding momentum traders, imposing price limits, or halving the retail population likewise leave δ within 10% of the baseline. This robustness is consistent with the empirical observation that δ ≈ 0.5 holds across markets with widely varying trading rules and participant mixes [6,3,4]. Three analytical frameworks predict δ from exponents that can be measured independently. We sketch each derivation's logic, identify its core assumption, and explain why that assumption fails in our model.

GGPS: δ = β -1.. Gabaix et al. [9] argue as follows. If metaorder sizes follow a power law P (Q > q) ∼ q -β and each unit of volume moves the price by a constant amount λ, then a metaorder of size Q causes impact I = λQ. The largest metaorder on a given day has and normalising by σ D gives Matching this against the empirical form -but this only reproduces the linear law. To obtain δ < 1, GGPS posit that large trades find progressively more hidden liquidity, effectively diluting per-unit impact to λ ∼ Q β-2 . Substituting into the normalisation yields δ = β -1. Why it fails. The prediction requires a pure power-law tail P (Q > q) ∼ q -β from which β can be estimated. In our simulation the metaorder size distribution (Figure 8, panel a) is only approximately Pareto -the tail bends due to the bounded [5, 50] child-order count -so the Hill estimator gives a well-defined β but its physical meaning as a tail exponent is questionable. Even granting the exponent, the hidden-liquidity dilution λ ∼ Q β-2 is an ad hoc assumption: it posits that per-unit impact decreases with order size, but provides no mechanism. In our model the dilution arises not from a sizedependent λ but from order splitting -a metaorder of size Q is broken into N c small slices, each encountering a quasi-stable book. The splitting mechanism, not the tail exponent, determines δ -consistent with Zarinelli et al.'s finding that impact depends on participation rate and execution duration, not size alone [14].

FGLW: δ = α -1.. Farmer et al. [10] replace the size distribution with the distribution of child-order counts N c . If P (N c > n) ∼ n -α and each child order displaces the mid-price by ∆p ∼ σ D /V D (one "tick" of impact), then the total impact I ∼ N c ∆p. The same normalisation argument as GGPS then gives δ = α -1. Why it fails. As with GGPS, the prediction relies on a well-defined powerlaw tail for N c (Figure 8, panel b), but the bounded range [5,50] imposed by the splitting algorithm produces a distribution that deviates from a pure power law. Beyond the distributional issue, the assumption ∆p ∼ const means every child order moves the price by the same amount. This would be correct if the LOB were static and all children had identical size. But the child volumes are drawn from a Dirichlet distribution (so they vary), and although HFT keeps the book quasi-stable (Figure 9), the mid-price drifts as execution proceeds, so later children encounter a shifted book. This breaks the proportionality I ∝ N c . LOB walking: δ = 1/(1+γ).. If the visible cumulative depth grows as V (q) ∼ q 1+γ with distance q from the mid-price, a single market order of size Q must walk through the book until V (q ⋆ ) = Q. Why it fails. The formula describes a single market order of size Q crossing the book at one instant. In our model, by contrast, a metaorder is split into N c child orders spaced by Poisson gaps. HFT agents replenish depleted levels between children (Figure 9), so no single child order walks far into the book. The cumulative impact is the sum of many small displacements, each absorbed by fresh liquidity, rather than the single traversal assumed by the formula. Our model produces γ ∈ [1.5, 3.6] (concentrated near-best-quote liquidity), predicting δ ∈ [0.2, 0.4] for a single-order walk. The measured δ ≈ 0.5 is higher because splitting prevents the book from being walked through in one pass. Summary.. The three theories fail for two reasons. First, the distributional assumptions do not hold: the simulated metaorder size and child-order count distributions are only approximately power-law (Figure 8), so the exponents β and α are not well-defined tail indices. Second, all three theories describe the impact of a single order of size Q on a given book state -they lack a mechanism for split execution. In our model, order splitting breaks a large trade into many small child orders, and HFT replenishment keeps the book quasi-stable between them (Figure 9). The cumulative impact is the sum of many small displacements absorbed by fresh liquidity, not a single traversal of the book. Within our model, this coupling of splitting and replenishment is the only mechanism that survives counterfactual ablation. It is consistent with the latent-liquidity picture of Donier et al. [12], in which a hidden liquidity profile continuously revealed by price diffusion yields δ = 1/2 independently of the visible γ; what we add is the agent-level identification of which components are causally necessary, obtained by removing each one in turn.

Several agent-based frameworks have reproduced the square-root law. Tóth et al. [4] showed that δ ≈ 1/2 follows from the interplay between sequential metaorder execution and the shape of the latent order book. Their analytical framework derives a locally linear supply/demand profile from the assumption of diffusive prices and Poisson order flow, confirmed by a numerical model. However, the framework does not decompose the mechanism into agent-level ingredients: there are no designated market makers or explicit splitting strategies, and the model cannot identify which components are causally necessary for δ ≈ 1/2. Mastromatteo et al. [11] extended the ε-intelligence framework with stimulated liquidity refill -where limit-order arrival responds to recent market-order activity -and confirmed concave impact across execution protocols, but did not decompose the mechanism into separable agent-level ingredients. Donier et al. [12] derived δ = 1/2 analytically from a latent liquidity framework, providing a continuum theory that bypasses agent-level detail entirely. Our model differs from these in three respects. First, it retains explicit institutional structure -metaorders are generated by dedicated agents that split large parent orders into sequences of child orders arriving as a Poisson process, while HFT agents provide two-sided liquidity with adaptive replenishment. This makes it possible to ablate each component independently (remove splitting, remove HFT, etc.) and measure the causal effect on δ -something a zero-intelligence model [15] with homogeneous agents cannot do. Second, the four agent types (institutional, HFT, retail, news) are motivated by real market ecology rather than mathematical convenience. The resulting order flow exhibits stylised facts -heavy-tailed returns, clustered volatility, concave impact -without being calibrated to any particular dataset. Third, we benchmark three competing quantitative predictions (GGPS, FGLW, LOB walking) on the same simulated data, treating the model as a computational stress test that complements the empirical approach of [16,14,17]. The contribution is therefore methodological rather than model-based: the ABM is a tool for causal dissection, not a proposed market model in its own right.

The tick-level return ACF(1) ≈ -0.35 is a genuine bid-ask bounce signature [13], but the model also exhibits weak longer-horizon mean reversion because it lacks an exogenous fundamental price. The visible LOB shape exponent γ ∈ [1.5, 3.6] is higher than the empirical γ ≈ 1, a consequence of the minimal agent ecology (see discussion above). Adding a richer mix of order-placement strategies could bring γ closer to 1, but doing so would also diminish the discriminatory power of the LOB walking stress test. Each stock is simulated in isolation, ignoring cross-asset correlations. Our metaorders are reconstructed ex post from consecutive same-agent trades, whereas empirical studies use proprietary execution data; the two identification procedures need not yield the same size distributions.

A minimal limit-order-book ABM with four heterogeneous agent types reproduces the square-root law of market impact (⟨δ⟩ = 0.539 across 2000 stocks, vs. ⟨δ⟩ = 0.489 on the TSE). Two lines of evidence identify the responsible mechanisms. First, counterfactual ablation shows that only the removal of order splitting (δ → 0.324) or of liquidity replenishment by market makers (δ → 0.386) breaks the SRL, while perturbations leaving both intact move δ by less than 10%. Order splitting and liquidity replenishment are thus jointly necessary for the SRL within this model; the splitting rule, momentum trading, price limits, and background liquidity level are dispensable. Second, a per-stock comparison of three theoretical predictions (GGPS, FGLW, LOB walking) against simulated δ rejects all three on identical data: distributionbased theories over-predict, visible-book-based theories under-predict. The failure of all three single-mechanism predictions, together with the ablation results, supports the view that the SRL arises from the coupling of splitting and replenishment, consistent with the latent liquidity picture [11,12]. = 1 and initial mid-price = 10 000.
